title: What continuing education do licensed insurance agents need in the US?
description: How US insurance producer CE works: NAIC model acts, the 4 credit annuity course, and verified Florida and New York hour rules, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: Insurance producer continuing education in the United States is set state by state, not federally. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) Producer Licensing Model Act ties license renewal to meeting state education requirements, and its annuity model regulation adds a one-time 4 credit annuity course. Hours then vary: Florida requires 24 hours every 2 years, including a 4 hour update course, while New York requires 15 credit hours per biennial licensing period.
keyTakeaways: There is no federal producer CE rule. Each state insurance department sets hours, topics and cycles under its own insurance code, and most follow the structure of the NAIC Producer Licensing Model Act (#218).

Under Model #218 Section 7B a producer license stays in effect only while the renewal fee is paid and resident education requirements are met by the due date; Section 16B lets a nonresident satisfy CE through their home state on a reciprocal basis.
The NAIC Suitability in Annuity Transactions Model Regulation (#275), revised in 2020, requires a one-time 4 credit annuity training course before selling annuities and makes the insurer verify it.
Florida (section 626.2815, Florida Statutes) requires a license-specific 4 hour update course plus 20 elective hours every 2 years, reduced to 16 elective hours after 6 years of licensure.

New York (Insurance Law section 2132) requires 15 credit hours per licensing period, including at least one hour each of insurance law, ethics, and diversity, inclusion and elimination of bias, plus flood content for property and casualty licensees.
jurisdiction: United States (state insurance regulation; NAIC model laws, with Florida and New York as verified examples)
regulator: State insurance departments, including the Florida Department of Financial Services and the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS), coordinating model laws through the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC)
appliesTo: Resident licensed insurance producers (agents and brokers) for lines that require a licensing examination
Nonresident producers, subject to home state reciprocity
Producers who sell annuities, for the one-time annuity training course
Insurers and appointing entities that must verify training or condition appointments on CE compliance

sections.heading: Who sets continuing education requirements for insurance producers?

blocks.text: Each state insurance department sets producer continuing education under its own insurance code; there is no federal standard. The NAIC, the standard-setting body of state insurance regulators, publishes model laws that states adopt in whole or in part, which is why requirements look similar in structure but differ in hours and topics.

The [NAIC Producer Licensing Model Act (#218)](https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/model-law-218.pdf) does not prescribe a number of hours. Instead it makes education a condition of keeping a license: Section 7B provides that a producer license remains in effect, unless revoked or suspended, "as long as the fee ... is paid and education requirements for resident individual producers are met by the due date." Section 7C lets a producer whose license lapses reinstate it within 12 months of the renewal due date without retaking the exam.

Model #218 also removes duplication for producers licensed in several states. Section 16B treats a nonresident's compliance with home state CE as compliance in the other state, if the home state reciprocates. Section 9 exempts producers licensed for the same lines elsewhere from prelicensing education and exams when they apply within 90 days of cancelling the prior license or move and apply for a resident license within 90 days of establishing residence.

sections.heading: What annuity training does the NAIC model require?

blocks.text: A producer who sells annuities must complete a one-time annuity training course worth at least 4 continuing education credits, in states that have adopted Section 7 of the [NAIC Suitability in Annuity Transactions Model Regulation (#275)](https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/model-law-275.pdf). The 2020 revision, often called the best interest standard, also requires producers who completed the earlier course to take a new 4 credit course or a 1 credit update within 6 months of their state's effective date.

blocks.title: Model #275, Section 7B(1)(a)
blocks.text: "A producer who engages in the sale of annuity products shall complete a one-time four (4) credit training course approved by the department of insurance and provided by the department of insurance-approved education provider."

Section 7B(3) fixes the course outline: types and classifications of annuities, the parties to an annuity, how contract features affect consumers, income taxation of qualified and non-qualified annuities, primary uses of annuities, and the standard of conduct, sales practices, replacement and disclosure requirements. Providers may not include marketing or sales technique content. Separately, Section 7A bars a producer from soliciting an annuity unless they meet the insurer's product training standards, and Section 7B(11) requires the insurer to verify the 4 credit course before allowing the producer to sell. Each state's adoption date and wording should be checked with its insurance department.

Florida requires most licensees to complete 24 hours every 2 years: a 4 hour update course specific to the license held, plus 20 hours of electives. The rule is [section 626.2815, Florida Statutes](https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0600-0699/0626/Sections/0626.2815.html), administered by the Florida Department of Financial Services, and applies to lines that require an examination for licensing.

items: **Update course content:** insurance law updates, ethics for insurance professionals, disciplinary trends and case studies, industry trends, premium discounts and suitability of products and services (626.2815(3)).

**Experienced licensees:** after 6 or more years of licensure the elective requirement drops to 16 hours, and further reductions apply to long-serving holders of certain designations or degrees (626.2815(3)(b) and (c)).

**Customer representatives** who are not licensed life or health agents need 6 hours; title insurance agents need 10 hours of Florida title and escrow content, including 3 hours on ethics, rules or compliance.
**Carry forward:** unlike many licensing regimes, excess hours in one 2 year compliance period may be carried into the next (626.2815(3)(g)).

**Appointments:** compliance is a condition precedent to issuing, continuing, reinstating or renewing an appointment (626.2815(4)), and the department may extend the deadline for good cause by no more than 1 year (626.2815(5)).

blocks.text: New York requires 15 credit hours of continuing education per licensing period to renew or relicense most agent and broker licenses. The hour count is in [New York Insurance Law section 2132(c)(1)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/ISC/2132), and the [New York State Department of Financial Services](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/apps_and_licensing/agents_and_brokers/continuing_education) sets the mandatory content for licenses renewing on or after April 1, 2022.

Within the 15 credits, NYDFS requires at least one hour of insurance law, one hour of ethics and professionalism, and one hour of diversity, inclusion and elimination of bias. Property and casualty licensees need at least one hour of flood insurance, and those who sell National Flood Insurance Program policies need at least three hours of enhanced flood content. Credits must be earned during the licensing period, which begins on the license's effective date, and must be completed before the renewal application is submitted.

Section 2132(b) exempts holders of licenses that do not require an examination and certain limited licensees. New York is a useful contrast with Florida: a lower hour count, but more prescribed topics, so a single national course catalog rarely fits both.

sections.heading: How can an insurer or agency map producer CE to evidence?

blocks.text: Insurers and agencies carry two kinds of duty: confirming individual producers stay licensed, and meeting their own verification duties such as the annuity training check. The table below is an illustrative mapping using the verified rules on this page; other states need their own rows.

blocks.text: The same producers usually also fall under an insurer's AML program: FinCEN's rule for insurance companies issuing covered products requires training of employees, agents and brokers, as set out on the [Bank Secrecy Act AML training](/regulations/bsa-aml-training-requirements) page. Building one [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) across licensing CE, annuity training and AML avoids three disconnected trackers.

sections.heading: How should firms handle producers licensed in many states?

blocks.text: Track the home state requirement first, because reciprocity under Model #218 Section 16B and statutes such as Florida's 626.2815(6) generally let nonresident licensees rely on home state compliance where the home state reciprocates. Then add the topic-specific items that do not travel, such as annuity training and state-specific flood or ethics content.

Cycles also differ: Florida runs 2 year compliance periods, while New York credits attach to each license's own period from its effective date. A refresh schedule built around each producer's renewal dates, rather than a single annual campaign, matches how departments actually test compliance; see [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles). Advisory staff who also hold securities registrations may owe [investment adviser representative continuing education](/regulations/investment-adviser-representative-continuing-education) on a calendar year cycle, and more on the sector is on the [financial services industry page](/industries/financial-services).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each state's producer requirements, the NAIC annuity outline and the insurer's own product training as separate obligations linked to the producers and lines they cover. Course completions then map back to the specific topic or hour requirement they satisfy, so verification and renewal evidence come from one framework rather than per-state spreadsheets.

faqs.q: Is there a national continuing education requirement for insurance agents?
faqs.a: No. Insurance licensing is regulated by the states. The NAIC publishes model laws, such as the Producer Licensing Model Act (#218) and the annuity suitability model (#275), but each state decides whether and how to adopt them and sets its own hour count, topics and cycle.

faqs.q: Do insurance CE hours carry over to the next period?
faqs.a: It depends on the state. Florida allows excess hours from one 2 year compliance period to be carried forward to the next under section 626.2815(3)(g). New York requires credits to be accumulated during the licensing period, with a limited allowance for relicensing. Check each state's rule.

faqs.q: Does the annuity training course count toward regular CE?
faqs.a: Model #275 requires the annuity course to be long enough to qualify for at least 4 CE credits and requires providers to register as CE providers, so in adopting states it is normally delivered as approved CE. Whether those credits also count toward the general renewal requirement is a matter of each state's CE rules.

faqs.q: Can a Florida producer get more time to finish CE?
faqs.a: Yes, for good cause. Section 626.2815(5) allows the Department of Financial Services to grant an extension, but no longer than 1 year. Licensees unable to comply because of active military duty may request a written waiver under section 626.2815(2).

NAIC Model #275 (Spring 2020 edition) Section 7: 7A product training standards; 7B(1)(a) one-time 4 credit course; 7B(2) at least 4 CE credits; 7B(3) six required topics; 7B(4) no marketing or sales techniques; 7B(6) new 4 credit or 1 credit update within 6 months; 7B(11) insurer verification.

Florida 626.2815(3): 4 hour license-specific update course every 2 years with listed topics; (3)(a) 20 elective hours; (3)(b) 16 hours after 6 or more years; (3)(d) customer representatives 6 hours; (3)(g) carry forward allowed; (3)(i) title agents 10 hours incl. 3 ethics/rules/compliance; (4) appointment condition; (5) extension up to 1 year; (6) nonresident reciprocity.

NYDFS: 15 CE credits to renew or relicense; at least one hour each of Insurance Law, ethics and professionalism, and diversity, inclusion and elimination of bias; one hour flood for P&C licensees; three hours enhanced flood for NFIP sellers; applies to licenses renewing on or after April 1, 2022; credits accumulated during licensing period beginning with license effective date.
New York Insurance Law 2132(c)(1): fifteen credit hours of instruction biennially; 2132(b) exemptions for licenses not requiring examination and certain limited licensees.
